extracted.intended_audience: student journalists and news reporters learning different types of news writing
extracted.subtask_short: writing news features and court stories
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for producing different kinds of newspaper stories (court reports, human-interest pieces, local angles, feature narratives), showing how the same facts can be treated in different ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring out human interest in routine news
rubrics_metrics.description: "The way in which the human interest can he brought out in what might ordinarily be considered routine news, is shown by the second of the following two stories."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use personal, emotional, and domestic details to turn an otherwise routine item (e.g., a patent decision, a probate notice, a business assignment) into a human-interest story. Example on page: the Janin hydro-aeroplane story emphasizes the inventor's poverty, family, celebration, and personal remarks to create an engaging narrative rather than a dry legal report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a local hook/angle from a small detail
rubrics_metrics.description: "The provision in the will given in the New York court story making bequests to Chicago nurses, formed the basis of the local story in the Chicago paper; both stories follow."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and amplify elements of a larger story that have local relevance (names, beneficiaries, institutions) and reframe the piece for a local readership. The textbook illustrates repackaging a New York probate item into a Chicago human-interest/local angle by focusing on Chicago nurses who received bequests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose treatment/angle — same facts, different approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: "How the same piece of news may be treated in different ways is illustrated in the following two stories."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide on an appropriate story form (straight legal/factual account, human-interest profile, local-angle piece, color feature). The text shows paired examples (e.g., New York Times vs. New York Evening World treatments of Janin) to demonstrate how emphasis, tone, and detail selection change the reader's experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct quotations from officials and principals
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories include verbatim statements such as Receiver Harrison's and Secretary Arthur's quoted remarks explaining causes and management intentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include named, on-the-record quotes from key actors (receivers, company officials, judges, relatives) to explain motives, justify actions, and add authority. Examples: Harrison's statement seeking authority to prevent loss; Arthur's explanation blaming the panic for business troubles; Janin and his wife's quoted remarks in the human-interest version.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide concrete numeric specifics (amounts, percentages, dates)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pages consistently supply figures (e.g., "$2,600,000 of the firm's paper", "the company has $600,000 in available cash", "$1,000,000 of preferred stock", percentages of share ownership).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify scale and impact with precise sums, percentages, dates, and estimates to give readers a clear sense of magnitude. Use these numbers in leads, context, and to contrast claims (estimates of liabilities, amounts bequeathed, stock percentages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Give background, history and biographical context
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-form background is provided (e.g., H. W. Williams' business history, prior consolidations, book-collecting, social standing) to contextualize current events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enrich news items by including relevant past events, career summaries, business ventures, and personal biography so readers understand causes and significance. The Williams bankruptcy story supplies extensive career and collection details to humanize and explain circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report legal/procedural status and court actions precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases such as "assigned yesterday for the benefit of his creditors", "admitted to probate", and "Judge Hinton ... made an order ... declaring the adoption ... void" appear as factual legal reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When covering courts and legal matters, state the procedural posture (filed, admitted, assigned, order issued, suit begun), names of courts and judges, parties, and specific relief sought or granted. These procedural facts are essential and often form the story's backbone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute sourcing and compare newspaper treatments
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories are headed with their source (e.g., "New York Times", "New York Evening World", "Kansas City Star", "Chicago Tribune") and the text shows differences between papers' versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always attribute the originating paper or wire service and, when useful, contrast how different outlets handle the same material to illustrate editorial choices. This is used pedagogically to teach angle selection and audience tailoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid descriptive detail and anecdote for color
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative details (e.g., Janin taking off his apron, the foreman wringing his hand, the description of the family flat and celebration) appear to enliven the report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concise, telling anecdotes and sensory details that create scenes and portraits of people involved. These elements make stories memorable and connect readers emotionally to subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain investigative findings and methods where relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: The business failure account explains that branch managers "juggled their reports" and that bankers "put an auditing firm upon the books" which discovered discrepancies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting scandals, failures, or financial trouble, describe how problems were uncovered (audits, bankers' suspicions, examinations) and what was found, so readers understand the evidentiary basis of allegations rather than merely assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead with a compelling opening that signals the chosen angle
rubrics_metrics.description: Example leads (e.g., the human-interest opener: "Albert S. Janin, cabinet maker, the other night took off his apron ... walked up to the foreman and resigned his job.") demonstrate opening with an arresting scene rather than a dry summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft the opening sentence to reflect the intended treatment — a human-interest narrative may open with a scene or quotation, while a straight court story may open with the legal action and parties. The lead sets reader expectations and tone.
